--- title: "Principal component analysis" description: "New axes built from old columns: what the loadings tell you, why 29% of the variance can be the whole signal, and why a component is almost never the gradient you were hoping for." order: 4 categories: [unsupervised] --- ## A map of twenty-four columns Twenty-four taxon columns cannot be plotted. You can look at them two at a time, which is 276 scatter plots, or you can look at correlations, which tells you about taxa and not about stations. What you actually want is a map: one picture in which similar stations sit near each other and you can see what makes them differ. Principal component analysis builds that map. It is the oldest and by some distance the most used unsupervised method in marine science, and the single most common error made with it is treating its axes as though they were the ecological gradients themselves. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. The R tab is what produced the tables and figures you see; the Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent, shown for translation rather than executed by the site. Figures stay in R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. It is real code, not pseudocode: it runs against the same files through `python/mlbasic_data.py`, and `python/check-snippets.py` executes every snippet in the site to keep it honest. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly**: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## The idea PCA constructs new variables, called **components**, that are weighted sums of your original columns. The first component is the weighted sum with the largest possible variance. The second is the largest-variance weighted sum that is uncorrelated with the first, and so on. There are as many components as columns, and they are ordered, so keeping the first two or three keeps as much of the spread as two or three numbers can hold. The weights are called **loadings**: one per original column per component, telling you how much that column contributes. The value of a component for a particular station is its **score**. Two properties follow and both matter later. Components are **orthogonal** to each other by construction, whether or not the real gradients in your data are. And the sign of a component is **arbitrary**: flipping every loading and every score gives an identical solution, so "high PC1" has no meaning until you look at the loadings. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The maths, if you want it Centre the columns of $X$ and take the eigen-decomposition of its covariance matrix $S = X^\top X / (n-1)$: $$S v_j = \lambda_j v_j , \qquad \lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \dots \ge \lambda_p$$ The eigenvector $v_j$ is the loading vector of component $j$, the score of station $i$ is $x_i^\top v_j$, and the eigenvalue $\lambda_j$ is the variance of that component. The proportion of variance explained is $\lambda_j / \sum_k \lambda_k$. If you standardised the columns first, $S$ is the correlation matrix, which is the usual choice, for exactly the reason [clustering needed it](clustering.qmd): otherwise the column with the biggest units wins. ::: ## Worked example ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() community <- load_coastal_community() taxa_only <- community |> dplyr::select(starts_with("tax")) prepared <- recipe(~ ., data = taxa_only) |> step_log(all_numeric_predictors(), offset = 1) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) |> prep() |> bake(new_data = NULL) pca <- prcomp(prepared) variance <- tibble(component = seq_along(pca$sdev), proportion = pca$sdev^2 / sum(pca$sdev^2)) |> mutate(cumulative = cumsum(proportion)) variance |> slice_head(n = 6) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| component| proportion| cumulative| |---------:|----------:|----------:| | 1| 0.159| 0.159| | 2| 0.135| 0.294| | 3| 0.062| 0.355| | 4| 0.049| 0.404| | 5| 0.045| 0.449| | 6| 0.044| 0.493|
::: ::: ## Python ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_community, load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() community = load_coastal_community() taxa_only = community.filter(like="tax") prepared = Pipeline([ ("log", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p, feature_names_out="one-to-one")), ("normalise", StandardScaler()), ]).fit_transform(taxa_only) pca = PCA().fit(prepared) scores = pca.transform(prepared) variance = pd.DataFrame({ "component": np.arange(1, pca.n_components_ + 1), "proportion": pca.explained_variance_ratio_, }) variance["cumulative"] = variance["proportion"].cumsum() variance.head(6).round(3) ``` ::: PC1 explains 15.9% of the variance and PC2 explains 13.5%, so the two together hold **29.4%**. By the standards of a textbook example that is a poor result. By the standards of a community matrix it is entirely ordinary, and here we can prove it is not a failure at all, because we know what went into this dataset. There are exactly **two** structures in it: a depth gradient and a hard/soft substrate split. Everything else is negative-binomial sampling noise, and three of the twenty-four taxa were given no response to anything whatsoever, so at minimum an eighth of the variance is guaranteed to be unexplainable. ::: {.callout-warning} "Percentage of variance explained" measures how much of the *total spread* the first components capture, not how much of the *signal* they capture. In sparse count data most of the spread is sampling noise, so a low percentage is expected and says nothing about whether the components are meaningful. Judge them by their loadings and by what they correlate with, not by their share. ::: ## Reading the loadings A component means whatever its loadings say it means. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} taxa_traits <- load_coastal_community_taxa() loadings <- tibble(taxon = rownames(pca$rotation), PC1 = pca$rotation[, 1], PC2 = pca$rotation[, 2]) |> left_join(taxa_traits, by = "taxon") ggplot(loadings, aes(PC1, PC2, colour = group)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]], linewidth = 0.3) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_text_repel(aes(label = depth_optimum_m), size = 3.1, seed = 1, show.legend = FALSE, na.rm = TRUE) + labs(x = "loading on PC1", y = "loading on PC2", colour = NULL, subtitle = "Labels are each taxon's true depth optimum (m)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Every taxon placed by its loading on the first two components, coloured by the role it was given when the data was generated and labelled with its depth optimum in metres. The three taxa built to respond to nothing sit at the origin.](principal-component-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-loadings-1.png){#fig-loadings fig-alt='Scatter plot of PC2 loading against PC1 loading, one point per taxon. The taxa lie around a ring centred on the origin. Position around the ring tracks the depth-optimum label: shallow taxa at the bottom right, working anticlockwise through the left side to the deepest at the top left. The six hard-substrate taxa occupy only the upper-right quarter of the ring, about a quarter-turn round from the soft-substrate taxa of similar depth. Three unlabelled points, the taxa built to respond to nothing, sit clustered tightly at the centre where both loadings are near zero.' width=1400} ::: ::: The taxa lie around a ring, and three things about where each one sits are correct. Position around the ring tracks the **depth optimum**: shallow taxa at the bottom right, sweeping anticlockwise to the deepest at the top left. So the depth gradient is in there. **Substrate group rotates a taxon round the ring** by roughly a quarter-turn: the six hard-substrate taxa occupy the upper-right quarter and nothing else does. So the substrate split is in there too. And the three taxa built to respond to nothing sit **on top of the origin**, loading near zero on both components: PCA gave no weight to columns carrying no shared signal, without being told which ones they were. A ring is what you get when two roughly orthogonal gradients are projected onto two axes. Each taxon's angle encodes which combination of depth and substrate it responds to, and its distance from the centre encodes how strongly. ## The direction the axes actually point Now the part that trips people up. It is tempting to look at that figure and name PC1 "the depth axis" and PC2 "the substrate axis", or some such. Check it against the truth. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} stations <- community |> mutate(PC1 = pca$x[, 1], PC2 = pca$x[, 2]) |> inner_join(dplyr::select(survey, station_id, depth_m, substrate), by = "station_id") |> mutate(bottom = if_else(substrate %in% c("rock", "gravel"), "hard", "soft")) tibble(against = c("depth (correlation)", "hard bottom (mean difference)"), PC1 = c(cor(stations$PC1, stations$depth_m), diff(rev(tapply(stations$PC1, stations$bottom, mean)))), PC2 = c(cor(stations$PC2, stations$depth_m), diff(rev(tapply(stations$PC2, stations$bottom, mean))))) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|against | PC1| PC2| |:-----------------------------|------:|-----:| |depth (correlation) | -0.666| 0.532| |hard bottom (mean difference) | 3.166| 2.316|
::: ::: ## Python ```python stations = community.assign(PC1=scores[:, 0], PC2=scores[:, 1]).merge( survey[["station_id", "depth_m", "substrate"]], on="station_id") stations["bottom"] = np.where(stations["substrate"].isin(["rock", "gravel"]), "hard", "soft") def against_bottom(column): means = stations.groupby("bottom")[column].mean() return means["hard"] - means["soft"] pd.DataFrame({ "against": ["depth (correlation)", "hard bottom (mean difference)"], "PC1": [stations["PC1"].corr(stations["depth_m"]), against_bottom("PC1")], "PC2": [stations["PC2"].corr(stations["depth_m"]), against_bottom("PC2")], }).round(3) ``` ::: Depth correlates $-0.67$ with PC1 **and** $+0.53$ with PC2. Hard-bottom stations sit 3.2 units higher than soft-bottom stations on PC1 **and** 2.3 units higher on PC2. Neither gradient belongs to either axis. Both are smeared diagonally across the pair. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} depth_direction <- coef(lm(scale(depth_m) ~ PC1 + PC2, data = stations))[-1] bottom_direction <- coef(lm((bottom == "hard") ~ PC1 + PC2, data = stations))[-1] tibble(gradient = c("depth", "hard bottom"), angle_from_PC1 = c(atan2(depth_direction[2], depth_direction[1]), atan2(bottom_direction[2], bottom_direction[1])) * 180 / pi) |> mutate(angle_from_PC1 = round(angle_from_PC1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|gradient | angle_from_PC1| |:-----------|--------------:| |depth | 139| |hard bottom | 41|
::: ::: ## Python ```python from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression axes = stations[["PC1", "PC2"]] depth_direction = LinearRegression().fit( axes, StandardScaler().fit_transform(stations[["depth_m"]]).ravel()).coef_ bottom_direction = LinearRegression().fit( axes, (stations["bottom"] == "hard").astype(float)).coef_ pd.DataFrame({ "gradient": ["depth", "hard bottom"], "angle_from_PC1": [ round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(depth_direction[1], depth_direction[0]))), round(np.degrees(np.arctan2(bottom_direction[1], bottom_direction[0]))), ], }) ``` ::: Depth increases along a direction 139° round from the PC1 axis; hard bottom increases along one at 41°. Both real gradients lie at roughly 45° to the principal axes, and at about 98° to each other, so nearly perpendicular, which is what they are in the survey. The reason is in the variance table. PC1 holds 15.9% and PC2 holds 13.5%: almost the same. When two independent gradients contribute nearly equal variance, *any* rotation of the plane containing them has an equally good claim to being "the largest-variance direction", and PCA's choice among them is arbitrary. It has faithfully recovered the two-dimensional plane the structure lives in, and it has no way to know which two lines in that plane you cared about. ::: {.callout-important} PCA finds the subspace, not the gradients. A component is a direction of large variance, and there is no reason for a direction of large variance to line up with an ecologically meaningful axis. When two drivers are comparable in strength, expect every component to be a blend of both. Naming PC1 after the variable it correlates with best is how plausible-sounding and wrong interpretations get into papers. ::: ## The station map With that established, the ordination itself is still the most useful picture in the section. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} arrows <- tibble(gradient = c("depth", "hard bottom"), x = 5 * c(depth_direction[1], bottom_direction[1]) / c(sqrt(sum(depth_direction^2)), sqrt(sum(bottom_direction^2))), y = 5 * c(depth_direction[2], bottom_direction[2]) / c(sqrt(sum(depth_direction^2)), sqrt(sum(bottom_direction^2)))) ggplot(stations, aes(PC1, PC2)) + geom_point(aes(colour = depth_m, shape = bottom), size = 1.9, alpha = 0.85) + geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = x, yend = y), arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm")), linewidth = 0.7, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) + geom_text(data = arrows, aes(x = 1.15 * x, y = 1.15 * y, label = gradient), colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]], size = 3.4) + scale_colour_viridis_c(name = "depth (m)") + labs(shape = NULL) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 800 stations on the first two components, shaded by depth and shaped by substrate. The arrows mark the directions in which depth and hard bottom actually increase; neither runs along an axis.](principal-component-analysis_files/figure-html/fig-ordination-1.png){#fig-ordination fig-alt='Scatter plot of PC2 against PC1 for 800 stations. Colour runs from dark purple for shallow stations to yellow for deep ones and forms a smooth ramp with no boundary anywhere along it. The cloud has two arms meeting near the origin. The lower-left arm is the soft-bottom stations, drawn as triangles, running from dark at the bottom centre up to the palest points at the far left. The upper-right arm is the hard-bottom stations, drawn as circles, running from dark at the centre right up towards the top. The two arms overlap only in a narrow band near the origin. Two labelled arrows leave the origin, one up and to the left marked depth and one up and to the right marked hard bottom, each at roughly forty-five degrees to the axes.' width=1400} ::: ::: The cloud has two arms meeting near the origin. The hard-bottom arm is a genuine boundary: it is what [clustering found](clustering.qmd), and the two arms overlap only in a narrow band. The depth shading, meanwhile, runs smoothly up each arm with no edge in it anywhere: that is a genuine gradient, and it is why clustering found nothing about depth until it was forced to. One ordination shows you both kinds of structure and distinguishes them, which is something no partition can do. ## Limits of PCA **PCA is linear.** It can only find structure that appears as a straight direction in the data. A taxon with a hump-shaped response to depth, which is most taxa including all of ours, is only approximately captured. Long gradients also tend to fold into a curve in the ordination, the *arch* or *horseshoe* effect, which ecologists have written about for decades. It is mild here because the gradient is short relative to the niche widths; on a full estuarine salinity gradient it would not be. **Variance is not importance.** A rare, patchily distributed taxon of high conservation interest contributes little variance and will barely register in any component. **Outliers dominate.** A single station with an enormous count, or a decimal-point error of the kind §2 hunted, can bend the first component towards itself. Look at the ordination for isolated points before interpreting anything. **The sign means nothing.** Re-run on another machine, or with a different BLAS, and PC1 may come out flipped. Never write "PC1 increases with depth" without saying which end you are looking at. ::: {.callout-tip} ## Key points - PCA makes new axes that are weighted sums of your columns, ordered by variance, each uncorrelated with the last. The weights are **loadings**; a station's values are **scores**. - **Standardise first** unless every column is already in comparable units. - 29.4% of variance in two components is not a bad result for a community matrix. Most of the rest is sampling noise, and here provably so. - Read a component from its **loadings**, never from its number. - **Components are not gradients.** Both real gradients here lie at about 45° to the principal axes, because they carry almost the same variance and PCA has no way to choose between rotations. - An ordination distinguishes a **boundary** (a separate lobe) from a **gradient** (a smooth ramp). That distinction is the point of the whole section. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run `prcomp()` on the raw counts with `scale. = FALSE`. Which single taxon dominates PC1, and what is its mean count? 2. Colour the ordination by `season` instead of depth. Season affects chlorophyll in this survey but was given no direct effect on the community: does the picture agree?
